summary: Defines performance cost metrics for ALTO, such as delay and loss, beyond the single generic routing cost metric in the base protocol, so applications can choose better resource providers.

plainLanguage.summary: When choosing which server to download from, you can ask for the fastest or least glitchy one, not just the nearest.

questions: how to ask for delay in alto
what are alto performance cost metrics
subtitle: Eight network performance metrics, from delay to bandwidth, that ALTO servers can offer instead of one generic cost.

tldr.problem: The ALTO base protocol (RFC 7285) defines only one cost metric, the generic routingcost, so an application cannot ask for the provider with lower delay or loss.
tldr.mechanism: RFC 9439 registers eight performance cost metrics (delay, delay variation, loss rate, hop count, TCP throughput, residual and available bandwidth) and adds an optional cost-context field that says whether a value is nominal, sla or an estimation.
tldr.outcome: ALTO clients can now ask a server for performance-based costs and know where the numbers came from. Servers may support any subset, and the values are sensitive ISP data.

today: RFC 9439 is a Proposed Standard published in August 2023, and the metadata lists no obsoleting or updating RFC. It builds on the ALTO base protocol in RFC 7285.

sections.title: Why ALTO Needs Performance Metrics
sections.content:
Application-Layer Traffic Optimization (ALTO) lets applications ask a network for information so they can pick efficient traffic patterns. Cost metrics are used by both the ALTO cost map service and the endpoint cost service in the base protocol, RFC 7285.

The base protocol set up an "ALTO Cost Metrics" registry so that different applications could use different metrics, but it registered only the generic routingcost. A delay-sensitive application had no standard latency metric to ask for, and a bandwidth-sensitive one had no bandwidth metric.

This document registers eight new metrics. Five are based on individual packets: one-way delay, round-trip delay, delay variation, loss rate and hop count. Three relate to bandwidth and throughput: TCP throughput, residual bandwidth and available bandwidth. Six of them are derived from the traffic engineering (TE) metrics already defined for OSPF, IS-IS and BGP-LS, extended from single links to whole paths.

All metrics are optional. A server announces the ones it supports in its information resource directory (IRD), and it may leave out metrics that raise privacy concerns. All metrics except round-trip delay are unidirectional, so a client that needs both directions has to query both.
sections.plainLanguage: Before, you could only ask a map service for "how far". Now you can also ask "how slow", "how bumpy" or "how wide" the road is, and the service can say which of those it knows.

sections.title: The cost-context Field
sections.content:
The same metric name can mean different things depending on where the number came from. RFC 9439 adds an optional cost-context object to the cost-type field of the base protocol. It holds a required cost-source string and an optional parameters value for details such as measurement settings.

Three source types are defined:

  • nominal: a value statically configured on the underlying devices. Throughput can have one, latency typically does not.
  • sla: a value derived from a commitment such as a Service Level Agreement. The parameters field SHOULD link to the SLA definition.
  • estimation: a value computed by an estimation process, for example from routing protocols, from measurement tools such as TWAMP, or from IP Performance Metrics (IPPM) frameworks.

If a metric carries no cost-source, the application MUST assume estimation, the most generic source. The cost-context is not used to tell metrics apart: an information resource MUST NOT announce several entries with the same cost-metric, cost-mode and cost-context.
sections.plainLanguage: It is like a label on a measurement: "measured just now", "promised in the contract" or "set on the machine". The number is the same kind of thing, but you trust each label differently.

sections.title: Statistical Operators
sections.content:
Measuring a metric usually gives a set of samples, not one value. RFC 9439 therefore lets a cost metric string have an optional statistical operator after a colon, as in delay-ow:min or delay-ow:p99. The whole string MUST NOT exceed 32 characters, the limit set by RFC 7285, so some long combinations cannot be expressed. The RFC suggests defining a shorter alias metric in that case.

The allowed operators are cur (the latest sample), min, max, median, mean, stddev, stdvar, and a percentile written as p plus a number from 0 to 100 with an optional decimal part, such as p99.9. Where a common form exists it is RECOMMENDED: use min instead of p0, median instead of p50 and max instead of p100.

With no operator, the default operator in the base metric's definition applies. If the base metric defines none, the value MUST be treated as the median.
sections.plainLanguage: If you timed a hundred bike rides, you could report the fastest, the slowest or the middle one. The suffix says which of these you are getting.

sections.title: Packet Performance Metrics
sections.content:
These five metrics describe the quality of experience of a stream of packets from a resource provider to a resource consumer. They are statistics over per-packet measurements: the delay, whether the packet was dropped, and the number of hops.

  • delay-ow: one-way delay, in microseconds, as the aggregation of link delays from source to destination. The number can be fractional.
  • delay-rt: round-trip delay, in microseconds, the sum of the one-way delays in both directions. A client could also query two delay-ow items itself, but the server should keep the values consistent.
  • delay-variation: jitter, in microseconds, measured relative to the minimum delay observed on the stream, which follows the networking convention rather than the statistical one.
  • lossrate: the percentage of packet losses.
  • hopcount: a non-negative integer number of hops. A hop is usually a router hop but may represent other units.

All values MUST be non-negative. For loss, the default aggregation, summing link loss rates, is valid only when link loss rates are low and loss events on different links are uncorrelated. For high but independent loss the RFC gives the formula of one minus the product of the success rates of each link.

For each metric the RFC also states which cost sources make sense. For example, delay typically has no nominal value, and hop count typically has neither a nominal nor an SLA value.
sections.plainLanguage: These are the things you could count about a stream of letters: how long each takes, how much the time wobbles, how many get lost and how many post offices they pass through.

sections.title: Throughput and Bandwidth Metrics
sections.content:
Three metrics describe how much traffic the path can carry from the source to the destination. All use bytes per second and non-negative values.

  • tput: the estimated throughput of a congestion-control-conforming TCP flow. It SHOULD be read only as an estimate and is designed for bulk flows. For an estimation source, the RFC recommends that parameters name the congestion control algorithm (for example by giving the URI of RFC 9438 for CUBIC) and the estimation method. Nominal and SLA values SHOULD NOT be generated for it.
  • bw-residual: the minimum residual bandwidth among all links on the path. Its default statistical operator is cur.
  • bw-available: the minimum available bandwidth among all links on the path, also defaulting to cur.

Bandwidth metrics use the minimum over the links because the narrowest link limits the path, whereas delay is a sum over the links.
sections.plainLanguage: A road is only as wide as its narrowest stretch, so for bandwidth the service reports the tightest spot on the whole route.

sections.title: Operational Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC leaves the measurement infrastructure and computation algorithms to each network, but it points out issues both servers and clients should expect.

Freshness. The metrics carry no timestamp. The server SHOULD return an HTTP Last-Modified value to show how fresh the data is, and it may use Expires to show when metrics will next be updated. A client that receives updates through incremental updates (RFC 8895) SHOULD treat the metric as a snapshot taken at roughly the receive time.

Backward compatibility. A client that does not know about cost-context would ignore it and could treat an SLA value as an estimation. To avoid trouble, if the metric is routingcost and it has a cost-context, the source MUST be estimation; otherwise the client SHOULD reject the information as invalid.

Aggregation. Routing protocols often report only per-link values, so the server has to combine them. Latency is the sum over the path, available bandwidth is the minimum, and loss is harder because losses on different links may be correlated.
sections.plainLanguage: Numbers go stale, so the server should say when it last looked. And since the older helpers do not understand the new labels, the labels are restricted so nobody gets fooled.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The document says its properties add no security considerations beyond those in Section 15 of RFC 7285, but that those concerns remain very important. TE performance data is highly sensitive ISP information, so sharing numerical values requires full mutual confidence between the server and client operators. The RFC expects servers to give such data to clients under strict and formal trust agreements.

To limit leaks, such as through person-in-the-middle attacks, the server should authenticate clients when it sends resources containing sensitive TE metrics. ALTO server and client implementations MUST support the https URI scheme and TLS (RFC 8446). Applications SHOULD also stop using ALTO guidance promptly if the data does not preserve, or even degrades, their performance.
sections.plainLanguage: How well a network works is private business information. It should only be shared with people the owner trusts, over a locked connection.

sections.title: IANA Registrations
sections.content:
IANA added the eight identifiers delay-ow, delay-rt, delay-variation, lossrate, hopcount, tput, bw-residual and bw-available to the "ALTO Cost Metrics" registry, each pointing to its section in this RFC.

IANA also created a new "ALTO Cost Source Types" registry. New types need IETF Review, and a request must include the identifier, intended semantics and security considerations. The initial entries are nominal, sla and estimation.
sections.plainLanguage: The official list of names got eight new entries, and a new list was started for the three kinds of label.
